howItWorks.intro: Score = (Mood + (11 − Anxiety) + Energy + Sleep + Social) ÷ 50 × 100. Each of the five inputs tops out at 10, so the maximum possible total before scaling is 50 — dividing by 50 and multiplying by 100 turns that raw sum into a 0-100 score you can track the same way from one day to the next. Anxiety is the one input that gets flipped: subtracting your rating from 11 means a high-anxiety day (say a 9) contributes almost nothing (2), while a calm day (a 2) contributes nearly the maximum (9). That inversion matters — anxiety and mood run on different tracks, and a wired, anxious day shouldn't score the same as a genuinely good one just because energy happens to be high too.

rules.name: Wellness Score
rules.explanation: Five-factor composite with anxiety inverted (lower is better).

howItWorks.outro: This is an equal-weighted average, not a validated psychometric scale — each of the five factors counts for exactly one-fifth because that's the simplest model to reason about and check by hand, not because sleep, energy, social contact, anxiety, and mood have been shown to weigh equally on wellbeing. For some people sleep dominates; for others, social contact does. Read the number as a rough daily marker worth watching over time, not a precise measurement of anything.

faq.question: Why track mood daily instead of just noticing when things feel off?
faq.answer: Memory for mood is unreliable — most people can recall that a week was rough but struggle to rank the individual days inside it accurately. Daily tracking replaces that guesswork with a timestamped record, which is why mood logs are standard homework in cognitive behavioral therapy: the log, not the recollection, becomes the data you and a therapist actually work from.

faq.question: Why is Anxiety inverted instead of just averaged like the others?
faq.answer: Anxiety and mood aren't the same axis. A high-anxiety day, rated close to 10, is a bad day for wellbeing and needs to pull the score down, not up. Subtracting your anxiety rating from 11 converts 'more anxious' into 'less contribution to the score,' which matches how anxiety actually behaves rather than treating it like just another positive factor.

faq.question: What does a low score, like 30 to 40, actually mean?
faq.answer: In this equal-weighted formula, a score in the 30s usually means two or three of the five inputs — most often sleep, energy, and social connection — were low on the same day. Treat it as a prompt to check which specific input dropped rather than a verdict on the day as a whole.

faq.question: Is this the same as a depression or mood disorder screening tool?
faq.answer: No. This is a self-reflection tracker built on a simple averaged formula, not a validated clinical instrument like the PHQ-9 or GAD-7, and it hasn't been tested against either. It can help you spot day-to-day patterns, but it can't diagnose anything. If low scores persist for more than a couple of weeks, or show up regardless of sleep, exercise, or social contact, that's worth raising with a doctor or therapist rather than tracking alone.

faq.question: How many days of data do I need before the score is useful?
faq.answer: Give it at least ten to fourteen consecutive days. A single entry is just a snapshot; the pattern across two weeks is what reveals whether your low days share a common cause, like a stretch of short sleep or a socially isolated week, versus being one-off bad days.

howWeCalculate.intro: Walk through one real day to see how the formula behaves. Say you slept poorly — six restless hours with a couple of wake-ups — so you'd rate Sleep Quality a 4. Work stress ran high most of the afternoon, putting Anxiety at 7. You skipped your workout and felt sluggish by evening, so Energy lands at 3. You mostly stayed in and only exchanged a few necessary messages, so Social Connection gets a 2. Taking stock at the end of the day, Overall Mood settles at 4. Plugging those into the formula: (4 + (11 − 7) + 3 + 4 + 2) ÷ 50 × 100 = (4 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 2) ÷ 50 × 100 = 17 ÷ 50 × 100 = 34. A score of 34 lands in the range that flags a genuinely rough day — not a crisis, but a day where sleep, movement, and contact with other people were all running low at the same time, a pattern a single mood rating on its own wouldn't have surfaced.
steps: Rate each of the five factors against your actual day, not how you think you should feel — six broken hours of sleep is a Sleep Quality of 4 or 5, not a 7.
Enter Anxiety the intuitive way, as how anxious you felt: a 9 means high anxiety. The calculator handles the inversion automatically so you never have to do the flip yourself.
The score computes the instant you click Calculate, entirely in your browser — nothing about your ratings is sent anywhere or stored.
Log the resulting score with the date somewhere you'll actually revisit it — a spreadsheet, a notes app, even a paper calendar — so a pattern has something to show up in after a week or two.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This 0-100 score is a self-reflection aid built from a simple weighted average, not a clinical or diagnostic instrument. It has not been validated against standardized screening tools such as the PHQ-9 or GAD-7, and it should not be used to diagnose or rule out a mood disorder. If low scores persist for more than two weeks, or you notice a pattern of low mood that shows up regardless of sleep, exercise, or social contact, talk to a doctor or mental health professional rather than relying on this calculator alone.

whenToUse.intro: This works best as a nightly five-minute habit rather than an occasional check-in — rate the day once it's mostly over, not mid-swing.
scenarios: At the end of the day, once you have a sense of how the whole day went rather than just how you feel in the exact moment you're rating it
Alongside an existing journaling or CBT thought-record habit, where the score becomes one more data point next to your written notes rather than a replacement for them
During a stretch when something in your routine has changed — a new sleep schedule, a new job, starting or stopping regular exercise — so you can watch whether the score moves with the change
Between therapy or counseling sessions, as a simple, low-effort way to bring concrete day-by-day numbers to a conversation instead of relying on how the whole week 'felt' in retrospect
When you realize you can't remember whether last week was better or worse than this one — logging removes the guesswork that memory introduces

sections.title: What Is the Daily Mood Tracker Score Calculator?
sections.body: This calculator turns five separate self-ratings — overall mood, anxiety, energy, sleep quality, and social connection — into a single 0-100 composite you can log once a day. Each factor uses the same 1-10 scale you'd find in a clinician's mood log, so a rough day doesn't require translating hours of sleep or number of conversations into anything unfamiliar. The number itself isn't the point; what matters is what shows up once you've logged it for two or three weeks and can see whether your low-energy days cluster around short sleep, isolated stretches, or spikes in anxiety. One entry tells you almost nothing. A month of entries starts to look like a fingerprint of what actually moves your mood.

sections.title: Why This Calculation Matters
sections.body: Cognitive behavioral therapy leans on daily mood logs precisely because memory is a bad historian — most people can recall that a week was hard but can't reliably rank individual days within it or say why one Tuesday differed from the next. Averaging five inputs instead of rating mood alone does two things a single number can't: it separates 'how do I feel' from 'what's driving how I feel' (sleep, movement, contact with people, stress), and it inverts the anxiety input so a calm day lifts the score the same way a solid night's sleep does. That inversion isn't cosmetic — without it, a wired, anxious 'high energy' day could score identically to a genuinely restful one. The formula stays deliberately simple, an equal-weighted average rather than a hidden model, so you can check by hand exactly which input moved the score.

sections.title: When Should You Use This Calculator?
sections.body: This is built for end-of-day use, not real-time mood checks — score the day as a whole, the way you'd write an evening journal entry, rather than mid-afternoon when you're still in the middle of it. It's most informative when used consistently: roughly the same time each evening, most days of the week, for at least ten to fourteen days before drawing any conclusions from the trend. It pairs well with a short written note of your own — the score tells you today was a 34 out of 100, your note tells you it was the day a deadline moved up and the gym got skipped. Neither one is complete without the other.

howToSteps.title: Rate your Overall Mood for the day (1-10)
howToSteps.description: Base this on the day as a whole rather than your mood in the last hour — a rough morning followed by a good evening might still average out to a 6 or 7.

howToSteps.title: Rate Anxiety, Energy, Sleep Quality, and Social Connection
howToSteps.description: Score each one independently: Anxiety on tension and racing thoughts, Energy on physical stamina and motivation, Sleep Quality on how rested you actually felt (not just hours in bed), and Social Connection on meaningful contact with other people, not messages sent.

howToSteps.title: Click Calculate
howToSteps.description: The calculator inverts your Anxiety rating automatically and averages all five inputs instantly in your browser.

howToSteps.title: Read the score in context, not in isolation
howToSteps.description: One score tells you where today landed on a 0-100 scale; the real signal shows up once you compare it against the scores from your last several entries and notice which inputs kept dropping together.

tips: Rate Sleep Quality on how rested you felt, not just hours in bed — eight fragmented hours often scores lower than six hours of unbroken sleep.

If Anxiety and Overall Mood always move in lockstep, you may be rating both off the same gut feeling. Try rating Anxiety first, based only on physical tension and racing thoughts, before you rate Mood.
A single day's score means very little on its own; the pattern across ten to fourteen consecutive days is what reveals whether low scores track with poor sleep, isolation, or something else entirely.

A Social Connection rating of 1 or 2 is worth flagging even when the other four inputs look fine — isolation tends to compound quietly over several days rather than showing up as an obvious single-day crash.

If you're rating retroactively because you forgot to log before bed, note that explicitly somewhere — same-day ratings hold up better than next-morning recollections, which tend to smooth over how the day actually felt in the moment.
